record.paper_title: Enabling and Emerging Technologies for Social Distancing: A Comprehensive Survey and Open Problems
record.original_question: How can traffic-light and traffic-flow scheduling for mixed pedestrian and vehicle networks incorporate social distancing directly, for example by reducing or constraining the peak number of pedestrians on the street at the same time instead of optimizing mainly for delay?

evidence.quote: Although there is a vast literature on traffic scheduling techniques, the social distancing implications have not been taken into account. For example, to maintain social distancing, a more meaningful objective would be to reduce/constrain the peak number of pedestrians on the street at the same time.

artifact.category_tag: traffic signal optimization with density constraints
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a mixed pedestrian–vehicle traffic network modeled as a directed graph $G=(V,E)$ in which each edge $e\in E$ represents either a road segment or a pedestrian sidewalk/crosswalk, and a subset $V_S\subseteq V$ of nodes are signalized intersections. At each signalized node $v\in V_S$, a traffic-light controller chooses a cyclic schedule $\sigma_v(t)$ that, at each time $t\in[0,T]$, assigns right-of-way to a subset of conflicting movements (vehicle phases and pedestrian crossing phases), subject to the usual feasibility constraints (minimum/maximum green times, clearance intervals, cycle length, and conflict-free phase assignment).

Given exogenous time-varying demands $\lambda^{	ext{veh}}_e(t)$ and $\lambda^{	ext{ped}}_e(t)$ for vehicles and pedestrians on each edge $e$, let $N^{	ext{ped}}_e(t;\sigma)$ denote the number of pedestrians simultaneously present on edge $e$ at time $t$ under the joint schedule $\sigma=(\sigma_v)_{v\in V_S}$, determined by a specified flow/queueing model (e.g., a point-queue or fluid model coupling arrivals, service induced by the signal, and walking speeds). Let $D(\sigma)$ denote the total expected vehicle-plus-pedestrian delay over $[0,T]$.

Fix a social-distancing capacity function $C_e\ge 0$ for each edge $e$ (representing the maximum number of pedestrians that can occupy $e$ while maintaining a prescribed minimum interpersonal distance).

Formulate and solve the following two scheduling problems, and characterize the trade-off between them:

(P1) Peak-pedestrian minimization:
\[
\min_{\sigma\ \text{feasible}}\ \max_{e\in E,\ t\in[0,T]} N^{\text{ped}}_e(t;\sigma).
\]

(P2) Delay minimization under density constraints:
\[
\min_{\sigma\ \text{feasible}}\ D(\sigma)\quad\text{subject to}\quad N^{\text{ped}}_e(t;\sigma)\le C_e\ \text{for all }e\in E,\ t\in[0,T].
\]

Specifically: (i) identify model assumptions under which (P1) and (P2) admit polynomial-time algorithms or provably good approximations; (ii) derive the Pareto frontier between expected total delay $D(\sigma)$ and the peak pedestrian density $\max_{e,t} N^{\text{ped}}_e(t;\sigma)$; and (iii) provide distributed signal-control policies (e.g., extensions of max-pressure or backpressure control) that achieve these objectives while remaining stable whenever feasible.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction in transportation/network engineering: existing traffic scheduling literature focuses on delay/throughput, and incorporating peak-pedestrian-density (social-distancing) constraints into signal control has not been systematically resolved. While related work on pedestrian-aware signal control and crowd-density-constrained scheduling has appeared since 2020, no widely accepted complete solution to the joint problem (Pareto trade-off, distributed optimal policies under density caps) has been established.
